conflicts.fact: Direction of phloem transport: whether it is downward only or bidirectional (source to sink)
conflicts.versions: Lesson 2 draws a single bold downward sugar arrow along the stem. Lesson 3 says phloem is bidirectional (source to sink, including to the cob). Lesson 5 says sugars travel mainly/downward through the phloem to roots. Lesson 8 says source to sink, including fruits and growing tips, and uses girdling evidence for downward flow.

conflicts.fact: Position of phloem relative to xylem in the stem, and bundle arrangement
conflicts.versions: Lesson 3 does not state a position, but Lesson 5 says xylem is inner and phloem outer, and it also has a ring arrangement in dicots, scattered in maize. Lesson 5's model-building phase says 'xylem inner/adaxial, phloem outer/abaxial', which is consistent with this, but Lesson 3's model has the two tissues as parallel lines from root to leaf tip, a simplification that conflicts with the stem-position structure.

conflicts.fact: Photograph C contents in Lesson 1 and the order of the celery dye experiment
conflicts.versions: Lesson 1 photograph C is described as sukuma wiki under mango shade but also includes 'moist soil around the maize in photograph A'. Lesson 5 says the celery dye experiment is set up at the end of Lesson 5 with results in Lesson 6, but its Observed section says students already observed initial uptake in Lesson 5, while Lesson 6 treats the dye cross-sections as a retrieval from Lesson 5.

conflicts.fact: Whether transpiration pull and cohesion-tension have been taught before Lesson 7
conflicts.versions: Lesson 5 says Lessons 1-4 covered the forces of osmosis and transpiration pull. Lesson 6 introduces transpiration pull in its Explained section, and Lesson 7 is titled and presented as the lesson introducing the transpiration pull/cohesion-tension 'engine', not covered in Lesson 4.

conflicts.fact: Energy requirement and role of root pressure / active transport
conflicts.versions: Lesson 3 says xylem needs no energy (passive). Lesson 4 says mineral salts enter roots by active transport requiring ATP. Lesson 7 says root pressure supplements the pull, which adds an energy-requiring push; xylem transport is described as purely passive in Lesson 3.

conflicts.fact: Cause of wilting near the riverbed and the soil water potential explanation
conflicts.versions: Lesson 4 says water enters only if soil water potential is higher than root hair cells, and that drier saline soil halts or reverses osmosis (no uptake). Lessons 6 and 7 say wilting is because transpiration exceeds uptake rate, assuming absorption continues; Lesson 8 combines both with 'root uptake less efficient'.

conflicts.fact: Why some plants die and do not recover
conflicts.versions: Lesson 5 explains irrecoverable wilting by xylem air embolisms (cavitation). Lesson 8 explains it by guard cells failing to close stomata or phloem compromised by drought, and never mentions cavitation.
